solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, enumeration length); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's answer wrong at 3 down, corrected here

clue.text: Instrumental being very short of delivery

definitions.note: used as a noun: an instrumental piece

indicators.note: something short is lacking its end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
natal means relating to birth, and a delivery is a birth

explanation.surface: Someone describes a musical piece played on instruments as falling a little short in its performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' reads as performance, but here it is childbirth, so 'of delivery' is NATAL, which loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonata is a classical composition for one or more instruments, so it is an instrumental work.

clue.text: Foil which holds with resistance in two places

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: 'that' can replace 'which' as a relative pronoun
W is the abbreviation for with
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone describes a metal foil gripping something with resistance at two points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In two places' tells you the outer word is broken twice: one insert goes after TH and another after A.
explanation.definitionFit: To foil a plan is to frustrate or block it, which is exactly what thwarting means.

clue.text: Device keeping kippers warm

blocks.note: surface reading: a kitchen gadget that keeps smoked herrings hot
setter's reading: a kipper is someone having a kip, a sleeper, and the device warms the bed

explanation.walkthrough: Kippers are smoked herrings, a British breakfast fish, but 'kip' is British slang for sleep, so kippers are sleepers.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated bedcover plugs into the mains and keeps people in bed cosy through the night.

clue.text: Fame having succeeded to bring down despot’s realm

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a letter down shifts it lower, so it is lifted out and set back further along

blocks.note: stardom is fame, the status of a celebrity
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in genealogies

explanation.surface: A celebrity's fame, once achieved, is used to topple a tyrant's kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The S at the top of the fame word drops one place, swapping with the T below it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was an absolute Russian ruler, and the suffix -dom names the territory he governed.

clue.text: Parisian article about monster clouds, very cool

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped round the rest

blocks.note: une is the French feminine indefinite article
a demon is a monster
strati is the plural of stratus, a layered cloud
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A French newspaper piece describes a monster obscuring the sky, which sounds very chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very cool' looks like the definition, but 'very' is V inside the French article; only 'cool' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cool in manner is reserved and unemotional, not showing feelings openly.

clue.text: Killing rodents, gathering one died beneath house

indicators.note: to gather is to collect something in, so one piece takes others inside

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
mice are small rodents
I is the Roman numeral one
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: Pest control: rodents are being killed, and one has died under the house.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'beneath house' means the house abbreviation sits on top, above the rodents.
explanation.definitionFit: Homicide is the act of one person killing another, a legal term for the deed.

clue.text: Nice bringing learner in for hour in game

indicators.note: bringing one thing in for another is a swap, so a letter is replaced

blocks.note: pheasant is a game bird shot for food
L is for learner, as on a British learner driver's L-plate
H is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: In the French city of Nice, a novice is brought in to play a game for an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is capitalised to look like the Riviera city; it is just the adjective. 'Game' here is wild birds, not a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice and pleasant are everyday synonyms for agreeable or enjoyable.

clue.text: Driving hazards inflamed Europeans according to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner was known for swapping the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: inflamed is hot and Europeans are Poles; swapping the opening sounds of the pair gives the spelling

explanation.surface: A warning about angry continental drivers being a menace on the roads.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the H and P sounds at the start of the two words to get the road hazard.
explanation.definitionFit: Holes in a road surface are a familiar danger to motorists, damaging tyres and suspension.

clue.text: Head north taking over dog’s lead

indicators.note: to take over is to replace whoever held the post, so one letter displaces another

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for north
a poodle is a breed of dog
the lead of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to go north, holding the dog's leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head north' looks like a direction to travel, and 'lead' like a leash; 'Head' is the definition and 'lead' is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodle is informal slang for a person's head or brain, as in 'use your noodle'.

clue.text: Help measure across back

indicators.note: going back means going the other way, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: dia is the abbreviation for diameter, the measure across a circle

explanation.surface: Someone asks for help measuring across their back.
explanation.walkthrough: Diameter is the straight-line measurement across a circle, abbreviated DIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid and help are synonyms, both as nouns and as verbs meaning to assist.

clue.text: Acrobat rider with arm on a bike’s front reversing

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept
reversing means going backwards, so the letters run in the opposite order
one thing on another sits beside it, so the later pieces are placed ahead of the earlier one

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of bike
a lancer is a cavalry soldier armed with a lance

explanation.surface: A circus performer rides a bike while holding something, then goes backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rider with arm' is a horseman with a weapon: arm means weapon, not a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrobat keeps poise on wires and poles, so a performer who balances fits the role.

clue.text: Wood, say, the Spanish pilgrim turned around

indicators.note: turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: el is the Spanish masculine definite article
a haji is a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca

explanation.surface: A Spanish pilgrim turns back in a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' looks like timber or a forest, but with 'say' it points to a person called Wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Elijah Wood is the American actor who played Frodo, so his first name is an example.

clue.text: Hybridised algae and broccoli, it’s connected to the study of bugs

definitions.text: connected to the study of bugs

indicators.note: a hybrid mixes up its parents' material, so these letters are recombined

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lab has crossbred algae with broccoli, and the result is linked to research on germs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' here means germs, not insects.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugs is informal for microbes, so the scientific field studying germs and infection fits.

clue.text: Half-cut staff regurgitated food

indicators.note: cutting something in half removes half of it, so only part of the letters remain

blocks.note: a cudgel is a short thick club, a staff

explanation.surface: Drunken employees are throwing up their dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk and 'staff' suggests employees; here it means halving a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Cows bring partly digested food back up from the stomach to chew again, and that is cud.

clue.text: Secure stuff with company, following being robbed

indicators.note: something robbed has had something taken from it, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: to pad is to stuff with soft material
a flock is a group or company of birds or people
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: After a burglary, someone locks up their belongings along with the firm's property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' is not CO here but a flock, which then loses its F.
explanation.definitionFit: To secure a gate or locker is to fasten it, and a padlock is the verb for doing that with a removable lock.

clue.text: Regeneration of this league club could be incalculable

indicators.note: regenerating something rebuilds it in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; it holds the letters of the answer plus those of the next fragment
taken as written, and taken away

explanation.surface: A football league club's revival could be worth an incalculable amount.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse construction: 'this' is the answer, and the answer plus CLUB rearranged would make 'incalculable'.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is a union of groups bound by agreement, which is what an alliance is.

clue.text: The French traitor shortly pointing implement

indicators.note: made short means cut off at the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: la is the French feminine definite article
a serpent is a treacherous person, from the snake in Eden

explanation.surface: A French traitor will soon be pointing a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' reads as 'soon', but it means the traitor word loses its tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Lecturers use a small handheld light beam to point at slides, so it is a pointing tool.

clue.text: Views of snake cults needing no introduction

indicators.note: with no introduction, the opening is missing, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: an asp is a venomous snake
sects are religious cults

explanation.surface: Opinions about snake-worshipping cults that are so famous they need no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing no introduction' sounds like praise for fame, but it means the first letter is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is an outlook or prospect, so views over a landscape or a matter are aspects.

clue.text: My rising vocal

indicators.note: vocal means spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a coup is an uprising that seizes power; its P is silent

explanation.surface: Someone notes their voice is going up in pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation of surprise, like 'Coo!' in British speech. The P in 'coup' is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Coo and my are both mild exclamations of astonishment in informal British English.

clue.text: Strange Med island bar I blunder around

indicators.note: bar means except, so a letter is left out
turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Ibiza is a Spanish island in the Mediterranean
taken as written, then removed
to err is to blunder

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to an odd blunder around a bar on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub on Ibiza, but it means 'except': drop the first I.
explanation.definitionFit: Bizarre and strange are synonyms for odd or weird.

clue.text: Stale pieces of bread in institution for vets

blocks.note: stale food is old
soldiers are British slang for strips of toast dipped in a boiled egg
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Stale bread is being served in a veterinary hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vets' looks like animal doctors, but it is short for veterans. 'In' is not a link word here; it supplies the last part.
explanation.definitionFit: A residential home for retired servicemen is an institution that houses military veterans.

clue.text: Gave speech and educated hosts

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the answer sits within the neighbouring words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, the whole second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A well-educated person gave a speech and entertained guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gave speech' looks like the definition phrase, but only 'Gave' defines; 'speech' is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand something over is to give it, so the past tense matches gave.

clue.text: We’d have recalled hiding this limb in reed

indicators.note: what is hidden sits inside something else, so stripping the outer wrapper leaves it

blocks.note: remembered means recalled
taken as written: these letters form the outside

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they would have remembered hiding a leg in the reeds.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse construction: put the answer ('this') inside REED and you get the word for recalled.
explanation.definitionFit: A member is a body part, especially an arm or leg, so it is a limb.

clue.text: In conversation, nobleman is unproductive

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so a word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a baron is a nobleman of the lowest rank in the British peerage

explanation.surface: Chatting about an aristocrat who never does any useful work.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are said the same way in most accents.
explanation.definitionFit: Barren land or effort yields nothing, so it is unproductive.

clue.text: Refusal to enter car, this writer’s free will

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece goes in between the others

blocks.note: auto is short for automobile
no is a refusal
the setter, as this writer, would say my

explanation.surface: The writer refuses to get into a car, asserting the right to choose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter, so its possessive is MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Autonomy is the freedom to govern oneself and act by one's own choice, close to free will.

clue.text: Man in charge of party picked up drink

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is taken by how it sounds

blocks.note: Keir Starmer leads the UK Labour Party

explanation.surface: The host of a party grabbed a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a celebration, but it is a political party: Keir Starmer leads Labour and is UK Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Kir is a French aperitif of white wine with blackcurrant liqueur, so it is a drink.

clue.text: Plan taking characters regularly in secret to cross border

indicators.note: taking characters at a regular interval means keeping every other letter
to cross is to go over and span, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters
a hem is the border of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: A plan involves passing secret messages across a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border' sounds like a national frontier, but it is the edge of a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a plan or plot for achieving something, often a crafty one.

clue.text: Test, perhaps, involving sheep on counter for judge

indicators.note: counter means opposite in direction, so the letters run the other way
to involve is to include, so one piece is wrapped round another

blocks.note: the Test is a river in Hampshire, England, famous for trout
a ewe is a female sheep

explanation.surface: At a farm show, an exam involves sheep displayed on a counter for a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test, perhaps' looks like an exam, but the Test is an English river, and 'perhaps' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer assesses books, films or work and gives a verdict, much as a judge does.
